sections.title: The digraph ch
paragraphs: The letters ch are a digraph. A digraph is two letters that together write one sound. The name sounds like ch in (chef) /ʃɛf/. Their main sound is in (chin) /tʃɪn/, which means the bottom part of your face. This digraph makes three different sounds, and it can also be a silent letter.

sections.title: Making the sounds
paragraphs: For the first sound, place your tongue tip against the ridge behind your upper teeth. Stop the air, then release it quickly through a narrow gap. For the second sound, touch the back of the roof of your mouth with the back of your tongue and burst the air out. For the third sound, push air through that narrow gap without stopping it. Keep your throat quiet for every sound.

sections.title: Reading the spellings
paragraphs: In most native English words, these letters make the sound in (rich) /rɪtʃ/. In words from Greek, they make the sound heard in (chemist) /kɛm.ɪst/ and (echo) /ɛk.oʊ/. In modern words borrowed from French, they make the sound in (machine) /mə.ʃin/. They are a silent letter in a few borrowed words, such as (yacht) /jɑt/.

sections.title: Common speaking errors
paragraphs: Do not mix the first sound with the third sound. Make sure you stop the air before you push it out in (chin) /tʃɪn/. Do not say the Greek words with the sound in (chef) /ʃɛf/. Remember to use the hard sound instead, as in (chemist) /kɛm.ɪst/. In the word (yacht) /jɑt/, do not pronounce these letters at all.
